justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'll assume was a current price near $118, with the 1-day estimate of $118.2 essentially anchoring close to the prevailing level given that very little directional information accumulates over a single session. The 1-week estimate of $118.8 and 1-month estimate of $120.0 incorporate a gentle positive drift, consistent with a baseline assumption of modest bullish momentum or mean reversion toward a slightly higher equilibrium. These estimates likely drew on recent price trend, any visible momentum in the underlying asset, and a default assumption that near-term macro conditions remain broadly stable without a major disrupting catalyst.

The confidence interval widths expand logically with time horizon, reflecting the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty that underlies most financial forecasting frameworks. At one day, the $2.70 half-width on either side reflects typical intraday-to-overnight volatility. By one week, the interval widens to roughly plus or minus $5.80, capturing the accumulation of daily noise across multiple sessions. The one-month interval of plus or minus $12 reflects that over four to five weeks, earnings announcements, macro data releases, sector rotations, and idiosyncratic news can compound substantially. Liquidity conditions and bid-ask dynamics also play a modest role in widening shorter-horizon intervals when markets are thin.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals include unexpected central bank communications or a surprise shift in interest rate expectations, which could trigger sharp repricing across correlated assets. A geopolitical shock, a significant earnings miss or beat from a market-moving company, or a sudden deterioration in credit conditions could all produce moves well beyond the stated bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon. On the upside, stronger-than-expected economic data or a resolution of an ongoing macro uncertainty could drive prices meaningfully above $132.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals, while calibrated to approximate 90% coverage, are model-dependent and subject to the limitation that financial returns exhibit fat tails. Realized volatility can spike suddenly in ways that Gaussian-based intervals underestimate, meaning the true probability of extreme outcomes is somewhat higher than the stated 10% outside the confidence bounds. Any structural break in the market regime — a liquidity crisis, a flash crash, or a sudden correlation breakdown — would render these estimates unreliable guides.
